utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good, Your Honour. This is case number IT-02-57-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a status conference in the case and the first thing I will do is take the appearances. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Peter McCloskey and Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Zoran Zivanovic for the Defence, for the Defence of Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Now, Mr. Popovic, could you stand for a moment? Are you able to hear the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Without prejudging the question of joinder I think it's fair to say that there's a measure of similarity between this case and the case of Beara, which is another case that I have responsibility for. My inclination is to follow similar courses of action to those which I ordered in relation to Beara. Now, in general terms, do you see anything wrong with that course of action?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have now an application to amend the indictment so that there is a consolidated amended indictment, I think, to be considered at some stage, and there was some delay in responding to that on the part of Mr. Popovic but that has been remedied now and I think there is a response, Mr. Zivanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We responded on the motion yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's the 21sth and that's a short delay over the time normally allocated. What I propose doing is simply extending the time for that response until the 21st, unless Mr. McCloskey has any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll do that. So that response is now before the Court. All right. Thank you. Now, I think although it's not within my control to deal with the joinder and these other outstanding motions, I anticipate that joinder will be dealt with first before the question of the amendment to the indictment. And it also seems appropriate to leave on hold the challenges to the existing indictment until we see what form the actual indictment takes. Do you agree with that, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So once the amendment is dealt with, if it's granted, then there will be time obviously for a challenge to be made to the final form and you would need to either repeat the challenges you've made or make fresh challenges in light of the new terms of that indictment. I think that deals with questions of outstanding issues other than questions of trial preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm remind there had is one other preliminary issue and that is the question of provisional release outstanding. The matter has been considered. A decision has not yet been made on that but it may be made later today or it may be made in fact it's likely to be made soon so -- but that will be intimated as a decision in writing because that's a matter for the Trial Chamber and not for me as an individual to deal with. That takes me to the trial preparation. Now, the supporting material was disclosed. The first issue, therefore, is the disclose of the statements that -- of the witnesses who are intended to be called. If that can now be done. Now, Mr. McCloskey, can that be dealt with in a similar way to Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, in fact it's practically been done already, all the Beara material has been provided and there may be a few additional that are more specific to this person. But like you said, they are very similar cases and as you may recall they were initially indicted or offered on the same indictment but Judge Schomburg decided to divide them up. So we have a few more witnesses but he's basically got everything from your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You I think indicated at the 65 ter conference that there are more witnesses, somewhere in the region of 20, and there are still issues over translation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There really not -- discuss this issue -- there are really not too much issues of translation at this point. There are a few witnesses that were not available to the Prosecution and are now available as Serbia becomes to cooperate more and over time there will be some witnesses that we get new statements from. But right now, when it comes to witnesses, we are practically up to date on translations. The only translation issues we have are the Drina Corps collection and we've actually had some movement on that. We have been given an earlier time frames -- well, helpfully from the last conference we had and appeals is under the same pressure so they have been able to put more resources into that collection and items are being translated as they are identified and that material is going -- will be going out to the Defence, and is, in fact, in bulk, already available to them but it's important for us to be able to get it to them in an indexed form with the most relevant items translated. And that is happening as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are a number of -- there are a number of 92 bis witnesses I think intended; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, this case is fundamentally -- been tried with some 50 to 60 witnesses. Now, many of those have already testified once, many twice. I basically, in looking over the Beara list, have pulled out nine for live testimony and have over 50 that I would like to put in as 92 bis, most of which have already been cross-examined and in the two trials -- fundamentally no one has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. really challenged these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked, though, in Beara to list those that would be 92 bis exclusively in writing, and those where you would intend to use transcripts of previous testimony, and those where possibly 89(F) might be used. Now, do you know if that was done in relation to Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Just a minute. We identified a few 89(F) and we said 92 bis and we have indicated whether or not they have testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But we didn't -- I don't think we distinguished whether or not we actually were intending to put in testimony or just a statement. But when they have testified, I prefer testimony because of -- they show that they were cross-examined and as you know, many of the judges here are concerned with the right to cross-examination, as they should be, so that's the way we normally do it. Now, that is going to put a huge burden on the Court to look at all this material. So I would say now that this -- one way to help get this case off the ground sooner is to try to get a 92 bis decision well in advance of trial and we will be ready to do whatever we need to do on that because that will save a tremendous amount of time or we'll find out that it won't save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I had in mind to make a similar order about disclose of these statements -- or intimation of these statements and to allow a similar period. That would be about a month from today. Is that the best way to proceed, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- we assume that and we are ready to do that. In fact, in regard to your agreed facts I think we've already provided the agreed facts to all counsel on all these cases, so we assume that and we are ready to do that and 30 days should be fine. We will be back in time to get that ready to be filed in the late part of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in relation to experts, is the position the same in this case also?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same -- the experts are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that means that you're in a position to deal with all the expert evidence, I think; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exactly what do you mean by deal with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you have reports or statements of all the expert witnesses. There is none of these outstanding, as I understand it. There was one suggestion of a demographic expert but you've even got that available now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we've had the demographic report, but like any report of this sort of science, it's best to have it updated because the figures are based on censuses, ICRC updates, things like that so we would like a small update. But fundamentally the numbers of missing which this report is based on are not going to change in any great deal. But it would be appropriate to have an updated report which we should be able to get to. I'm speaking to the demographer today to get -- I hope to give her an October 1 deadline for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you disclosed what you have so far any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh yes. Yes, they have had that and the demographers have been cross-examined and the fundamental issues have not changed at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And reverting to the statement of agreed -- of proposed agreed facts, could you let the Trial Chamber also have a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see that, you see, as forming a sort of an agenda for the Senior Legal Officer at the next 65 ter conference to try to five the prospects of coming together on material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We will provide that to the Court. It was not a formal part of your order, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No it wasn't but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But we'll get that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, that was not covered, but I would like to have that available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One other expert, Your Honour, Your Honours, the military expert which -- again, the bulk of the report has been done and it's been finished and cross-examined on but with this new Drina Corps collection, we will have a short update to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the proposed date for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That again is dependent on this collection being finished. So if they are true to their word that September it's going to get finished, I'll press my expert. He unfortunately no longer works for the UN. He's now working in his home country. But I hope certainly before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 1st of October sounded much better to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Demographics are in house and I've got a much better hammer on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But military experts are vital and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it will assist me to offer your views to the expert on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may even appear in an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was afraid of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zivanovic, I was told that there may be an issue over the ability of the accused, Mr. Popovic, to have access to equipment on which he can read the disclosed material which has been provided in the form of a DVD or a number of DVDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you clarified that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I try to solve this problem with the United Nations Detention Unit and with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it has not yet been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it Mr. Popovic's intention to make use of the electronic facility, if he can do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I believe he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some people are reluctant to do it but he's quite happy to do it, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked him and you can ask him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. I would rather you told me. I'm content Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with you. As far as you understand, he will try to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he will be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If he could have the equipment to monitor this -- to watch the DVDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the final matter that at least I have noted is the disclosure of exculpatory material. Are you happy that the Prosecution are making adequate efforts to identify and disclose to you anything that may be helpful to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I believe that the Prosecution has the obligation under Rule 68 to indicate the exculpatory material, and it is not enough to give the access to EDS only, because it has a bulk of material absolutely irrelevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McCloskey, how do you address that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's important to realise that EDS is -- we are not providing -- saying here are all the collections, here is all this stuff, here is your search engine, do it. That's not our intention at all. What we are providing counsel as well as that ability are particularly indexes for the relevant military documents on the key dates, and the relevant witnesses both Serb and Muslims that on the key points. And we are intending to provide that for the entire investigation in an organised format so they can see it all. Now, I've gone through years and years of Rule 68 and watched the development of the law there and have experienced that practically all the VRS statements can be interpreted in one way or another as Rule 68, and almost all the witness statements that are relevant on point can go to the credibility of either that witness or another witness. So the best way that I have found to be able to solve my Rule 68 problem is to give this -- give the key witnesses and the key exhibits to the Defence and identify the material and get it on my witness list. Fundamentally, exculpatory material that actually shows that Colonel Popovic is not guilty or not involved in this, I don't have any. Do I have information that affects the credibility of witnesses? Yes. And that is all going to counsel. And if there is anything that is more significant than the usual, we will alert him to that. And I'm certainly willing to sit down and talk with him about the various issues and -- that have come up, and identify things for him in that regard, and we will meet our Rule 68 obligation. As I see things that are absolutely exculpatory or go directly to credibility, we will provide that to him and alert him to it. But the best way to do this is to give him access to the key Serb statements and the key documents because any lawyer worth his salt can look at a key document and find a way that it supports his case and that's been my experience here. So that's the way we did it in the last trial, Defence counsel was very satisfied. Each Defence counsel is different. But we will keep an eye out and we do keep an eye out and we do search normally for exculpatory material because that's the material that the Court will see and will want us to resolve at trial. So we have an ongoing not only duty but every reason in the world to do this and we will continue to do it. The team does it all day, every day, and -- but fundamentally, obvious, exculpatory material that shows he's not guilty, just don't see much of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've actually no direct experience of the operation of electronic disclosure system but I intend -- in fact I intended yesterday to try to acquire some familiarity with it. I was unable to do so but I intend to do so very soon. And I do know what the general nature of the complaints made by the Defence and by Defence counsel about the difficulty of identifying helpful material because of the lack of indices within the system. So I will have a look at it. But it seems to me, Mr. Zivanovic, that it's a very reasonable suggestion that Mr. McCloskey makes that he's willing to sit down with you and look at the issues. I think in the first instance, bearing in mind the nature of the system, the size of it, the quantity of material, that that must be the first stage, that you need to identify areas that you're particularly interested in and enlist Mr. McCloskey's assistance. And I'll be sympathetic to submissions about difficulties in that regard at the next status conference. What I'm proposing to do is to align this case with the case of Beara. If in fact the motion for joinder is granted then the status conference can take place together and bearing in mind that possibility, I'm going to fix the next status conference for this case for the same date, although it's quite soon. Nevertheless, I think it's going to be suitable because there should be -- a lot should have happened between now and then. The Is should be dotted, the Ts crossed in relation to disclosure. It doesn't need a lot of time for that to be done. And I anticipate at the next status conference ordering the pre-trial brief as well. So I don't think we need to wait to November for that in this case. And the date we have already for the other status conference is the 21st of September. Now, you'll be notified about the time nearer the time. It will be the afternoon, but whether it's separate from or along with that of Colonel Beara will depend on circumstances between now and then. Now, is there any other issue you want me to address this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing at the moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, is there any matter that you personally wish to raise with me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my surgery, it seems to me that everything went fine. Now, as for the diabetes, the elevated levels of sugar in my blood that I developed after arriving here, I think that I would probably need more check-ups and monitoring by specialists but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I certainly have every confidence in the detention unit to arrange any necessary medical examination and treatment. But you know that it is always open to you, should you have any concern about the way you're being treated, to raise that matter either personally, directly, with the Detention Unit or through your counsel with the Pre-Trial Chamber and with me in particular. That facility is available to you. It doesn't just exist on the days when you actually come to court. Well, I'm very grateful to counsel for their assistance. What I shall do is issue a brief order confirming the various things that have been done in the course of this status conference. That will be issued later today. I confirm that the next status conference will be on the 21st of September and I now adjourn this hearing.
